questions.q: Imran sits facing outwards on a playground merry-go-round that a friend turns slowly clockwise (seen from above). He keeps his eyes on one tree. How does the tree appear to move, and on which side of him does it come into view?
questions.a: Anticlockwise around him, coming into view on his right and leaving on his left. The book's ride turns anticlockwise and the tree then seems to turn clockwise, entering on the left and leaving on the right; turning the ride the other way reverses both.
o: Anticlockwise around him, coming into view on his right and leaving on his left
Clockwise around him, coming into view on his left and leaving on his right
Anticlockwise around him, coming into view on his left and leaving on his right
Clockwise around him, coming into view on his right and leaving on his left

questions.q: Pooja in Rajkot is having lunch under a bright midday Sun. Her cousin lives at the place on the opposite side of the Earth, at the other end of a line through the Earth's centre. What is the situation there at that moment?
questions.a: It is night there. Sunlight falls on only half of the Earth at a time; a place in the middle of the lit half has its opposite place in the middle of the dark half.
o: It is night there, because that place lies in the half of the Earth that the Sun's light does not reach
It is day there too, because the Sun's light reaches every part of the Earth at once
It is evening there, because the Earth finishes one rotation in only 12 hours
It is morning there, because that place has just turned into the lit half

questions.q: A globe is turned from West to East under a fixed torch. Light has just begun to touch the sticker on Ahmedabad (sunrise there). What is true of the sticker on Dibrugarh, which lies far to the east of Ahmedabad?
questions.a: It moved into the lit half earlier, so it is already in daytime. On a globe turned West to East, light falls on eastern places first.
o: It moved into the lit half earlier, so it is already in daytime
It is still in the dark half, because the light reaches the east last
It is entering the light at the same moment, because both places are in India
It has already left the lit half and is in night-time

questions.q: Neel writes in his notebook: 'We have night because the Earth revolves around the Sun once every 24 hours.' Which correction is right?
questions.a: Night comes from the Earth's rotation on its own axis in about 24 hours; revolution around the Sun takes about 365 days and 6 hours.
o: Night comes from the Earth's rotation in about 24 hours; revolution takes about a year
Night comes because the Moon covers the Sun every evening for some hours, as in an eclipse
The sentence is right, but revolution around the Sun takes only about 12 hours for the Earth
Night comes because the Earth's axis tilts away from the Sun every evening and back each morning

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Earth's rotation.
1. Seen from above the North Pole, the Earth turns clockwise.
2. A place experiences sunrise when it turns from the dark half into the lit half.
3. A rider on an anticlockwise merry-go-round sees a nearby tree turn clockwise around her.
questions.a: 2 and 3 only. Statement 1 is false: seen from above the North Pole the Earth turns anticlockwise, that is West to East.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Sun appears to rise in the East and set in the West.
Reason (R): The Sun travels around the Earth once in about 24 hours.
questions.a: A is true but R is false. The Sun only appears to move; the Earth turns once in about 24 hours.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column A with the idea it shows in Column B.
Column A:
1. A rider sees a fixed tree turn round her
2. The half of a globe that faces the torch
3. A sticker on the globe returns to its starting place
4. A metal rod through the two poles of a globe
Column B:
a. Daytime on that half
b. The axis of rotation
c. Apparent motion caused by the observer's own turning
d. One rotation, taking the Earth about 24 hours
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-d, 4-b. The tree's turning is apparent, the lit half is day, a full return is one rotation and the rod marks the axis.

questions.q: An expedition leaves at 6 am on a Monday and returns at 6 am on the Friday of the same week. During the expedition the Earth completes ___ rotations.
True or False, with a reason: if the Earth rotated from East to West instead of West to East, the Sun would appear to rise in the West and set in the East.
questions.a: True. The Sun's apparent motion is always opposite to the direction in which the observer's Earth turns, as the trees seem to turn opposite to a merry-go-round. Reversing the rotation would reverse the apparent path of the Sun.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: apparent motion is opposite to the Earth's turning, so reversing the rotation reverses it

questions.q: Meera stands on the Equator facing North and sees the morning Sun rising on her right. (a) On which side of her does the Sun set in the evening? (b) If she turns to face South instead, on which side of her does she see it set?
questions.a: (a) On her left, because West is on her left when she faces North. (b) On her right, because facing South puts West on her right.
s: Part (a): sets on her left, West being on the left when facing North
Part (b): sets on her right when she faces South

questions.q: A planet is found to turn once on its axis in 30 hours. (a) How many complete day-night cycles does a place on it have in one Earth week of 168 hours? (b) How many hours of that week are left over after those cycles?
questions.a: (a) 168 / 30 = 5.6, so 5 complete cycles (one rotation gives one day-night cycle). (b) 168 - 5 x 30 = 18 hours.
s: Part (a): 5 complete cycles, one per rotation
Part (b): 18 hours left over

questions.q: A student says the Sun 'goes down' at sunset and 'comes up' at sunrise. Rewrite both events in terms of what the Earth and the place on it do, using the words lit half and dark half.
questions.a: At sunrise the place, carried by the Earth's rotation, turns from the dark half into the lit half. At sunset it turns from the lit half into the dark half. The Sun is not going down or up; the place is turning.
s: Sunrise: the place turns into the lit half
Sunset: the place turns into the dark half, and the cause is the Earth's turning

questions.q: Differentiate between what really moves and what only appears to move (i) when you ride a merry-go-round and look at the trees, and (ii) when you watch the Sun cross the sky.
questions.a: (i) The rider really moves (turns with the ride); the trees are fixed but appear to turn the opposite way. (ii) The Earth with the observer on it really turns from West to East; the Sun appears to move from East to West.
s: Merry-go-round: the rider moves, the trees only appear to
Sun: the observer on the rotating Earth moves, the Sun's crossing is apparent

questions.q: Give an example of rotation from daily life that is not mentioned in the chapter. Name the axis of rotation and say how the parts of the object move.
questions.a: For example a ceiling fan or a potter's wheel. Its axis is an imaginary line through its centre; all its parts move in circles around that line.
s: Gives a valid example of rotation
Identifies the imaginary axis through the object
Says all parts move in circles around the axis

questions.q: Ananya says, 'Night comes because the Moon moves in front of the Sun every evening, as in an eclipse.' Do you agree? Give two points from the chapter.
questions.a: No. Night comes because the Earth's rotation carries the place into the half that sunlight does not reach; this happens every day. A solar eclipse is a different event: the Moon blocks the Sun only at certain times and the total darkness lasts a few minutes, while night lasts for hours.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Gives the cause of night: the place turns into the dark half by rotation
Separates it from an eclipse, a rare and short event

questions.q: Show that Kohima in the far east and Rajkot in the west cannot have sunrise at exactly the same instant. Use the globe-and-torch activity in your argument.
questions.a: In the activity the light falls on the eastern part of India first when the globe is turned West to East. So the eastern place enters the lit half before the western place. Light reaches the two places one after the other, so their sunrises cannot be at the same instant.
s: States that light reaches the east first when the globe turns West to East
Says the eastern place enters the lit half before the western place
Concludes the sunrises are at different times

questions.q: A girl stands on the Equator facing South while the Earth rotates. Describe, in order, where she sees the Sun in the morning, at noon and in the evening, and what she sees after that. Explain why her view is a mirror image of a girl facing North.
questions.a: Facing South, the East is on her left and the West on her right. In the morning the Sun appears on her left, in the East. Around noon it is overhead. In the evening it sets on her right, in the West. Then stars become visible. The girl facing North has East on her right, so her view is reversed left-right, but both see the Sun rise in the East and set in the West because the Earth rotates West to East.
s: Morning: Sun on her left, in the East
Noon: Sun overhead
Evening: Sun on her right, in the West
After sunset: stars visible
Explains the left-right reversal with the same East-to-West apparent motion

questions.q: You must design a model using a globe, a torch, a sticker and a dark room for the science fair. Describe how you will set it up and use it to show (i) day and night at your own place, (ii) sunrise reaching the east of India first, and (iii) why the Sun seems to cross the sky from East to West to a person on the globe.
questions.a: Set the globe about 1.5 m from the torch in a dark room; half the globe is lit (day) and half dark (night). Put the sticker on your place. Turn the globe slowly from West to East: the sticker passes into light (sunrise) and into dark (sunset), and returns to the start after one rotation of about 24 hours. Watch the east of India: it receives the light first only for West-to-East turning. For (iii) a person on the globe is the turning one, like the rider on the merry-go-round, so the Sun, which is fixed, appears to go the opposite way, from East to West.
s: Set-up: torch about 1.5 m away, dark room, half lit and half dark
Day and night: the sticker moves between lit and dark halves in one rotation
Sunrise order: turning West to East lights the east of India first
Apparent Sun motion: the observer is the one turning, as on the merry-go-round
Names the direction of turning and links one rotation to about 24 hours

questions.q:
Tanvi lives in Jorhat, Assam, and her cousin Hetal in Dwarka, Gujarat. On one winter morning the newspaper gives sunrise at Jorhat as 6:00 am and at Dwarka as 7:35 am. The teacher asks the class to treat the Earth as turning steadily through 360 degrees in 24 hours from West to East. Place Z lies 5 degrees of turning to the east of Jorhat. For the science fair the class must pick ONE model that (i) shows the order of sunrise and day-night and (ii) shows that the people on the surface are what move. Model X: a globe turned West to East under a fixed torch. Model Y: a torch carried round a fixed globe from East to West.
(a) Through how many degrees does the Earth turn in one hour?
(b) At what time does the Sun rise at Z on the same morning?
(c) Through how many degrees of turning do the sunrises at Jorhat and Dwarka differ, and is Dwarka east or west of Jorhat?
(d) Which model should the class pick, and which of the two requirements does the other one fail?
questions.a: (a) 360 / 24 = 15 degrees per hour. (b) 5 degrees takes 5/15 h = 20 minutes, and eastern places get the Sun first, so sunrise at Z is at 5:40 am. (c) 1 h 35 min = 95 min = 23.75 degrees; Dwarka sees the Sun later, so it is to the west of Jorhat. (d) Model X; Model Y meets requirement (i) but makes the Sun the mover, so it fails (ii).
s: Part (a): 15 degrees per hour
Part (b): 20 minutes earlier, 5:40 am
Part (c): 23.75 degrees, Dwarka is west
Part (d): Model X; Y fails the requirement that the surface moves

questions.q:
Kabir sits facing outwards on the school merry-go-round, which is turned slowly anticlockwise seen from above. A painted tree on the fence comes into his view on his left and leaves on his right. The Class VII teacher offers two models for the fair. Model P: a globe lit by a torch from 1.5 m in a dark room, turned by hand. Model Q: Kabir on the merry-go-round with a lamp on a fence post as the Sun, the audience asking him what he sees.
(a) If the painted tree stands for the rising and setting Sun, which compass direction would a girl on the Earth have to face to see the Sun come in on her left and leave on her right?
(b) The ride is turned twice as fast. What changes and what stays the same in what Kabir sees, and what does this correspond to for a faster-turning Earth?
(c) In Model P, what do the lit half and the dark half stand for, and in which direction must it be turned so that eastern India gets light first?
(d) A visitor wants to know (i) why the east of India has sunrise before the west and (ii) why the Sun seems to travel across the sky. Which model suits each question better? Is one model enough for both?
questions.a: (a) South: facing South, East is on the left and West on the right. (b) The tree still enters on his left, but returns twice as often; a faster-turning Earth would have a shorter day-night cycle. (c) Lit half is day, dark half is night; turn West to East. (d) Model P suits (i) since it shows places entering the light in order; Model Q suits (ii) since the rider experiences the apparent motion. Neither alone is enough: P cannot show how things look from the surface and Q has no lit and dark halves.
s: Part (a): South
Part (b): side unchanged, repeats twice as often, shorter day-night cycle
Part (c): lit half is day, dark half is night; turn West to East
Part (d): P for sunrise order, Q for apparent motion; judges neither enough alone

questions.q: At 8 pm Radha sees the Moon low above the eastern horizon from her roof in Surat. She keeps watching it through the night. Which description of what she will see is correct, and why?
questions.a: It climbs and drifts westward. Like the Sun, the Moon appears to rise in the East and set in the West because the Earth rotates from West to East.
o: It climbs and drifts westward, because the Earth rotates from West to East
It climbs and drifts eastward, because the Earth rotates from East to West
It stays near the eastern horizon, because only stars move across the sky
It sinks back below the eastern horizon, because the Moon revolves faster than the Earth rotates

questions.q: In a long-exposure photograph of the northern sky taken in Pune, the Pole Star is a dot while other stars are arcs. A classmate says, 'It is a dot because it is the brightest star in the sky.' Which reply is correct?
questions.a: Brightness has no role. The Earth's axis of rotation points very close to the Pole Star, so it appears nearly stationary while the other stars appear to move around it.
o: Brightness has no role; the Earth's axis points very close to it, so it hardly seems to move
Brightness is the reason, since a bright star outshines the motion of the sky and looks fixed to the eye
It is a dot because it is the nearest star and so does not share the Earth's rotation with the others
It is a dot because it revolves around the Big Dipper once every night, staying at the centre

questions.q: Ishita starts her star-sketching at 9 pm and draws the Big Dipper every two hours. She wants her record on one night to run for at least 8 hours. How many sketches will she have made when she finishes, and at what time is the last one?
questions.a: 5 sketches, the last at 5 am. Sketches at 9 pm, 11 pm, 1 am, 3 am and 5 am cover 8 hours (4 gaps of 2 hours).
o: 5 sketches, the last at 5 am
4 sketches, the last at 3 am
5 sketches, the last at 3 am
6 sketches, the last at 7 am

questions.q: Four visitors read a plate beside the 22-metre pendulum under the skylight of the new Parliament building in Delhi, named after Leon Foucault. Which visitor draws the correct conclusion from what the chapter says?
questions.a: It is the first simple demonstration of the Earth's rotation. Galileo found a property of the pendulum and Huygens used it for clocks; Foucault's long pendulum showed rotation.
o: It is the first simple demonstration of the Earth's rotation, given by Foucault in the mid-nineteenth century
It is a giant pendulum clock, built by Galileo soon after he found an important property of the pendulum
It shows that the Earth revolves around the Sun in about a year, as Foucault proved with a long string and bob
It was invented by Huygens to measure how long one rotation of the Earth takes, using a heavy bob

questions.q: A camera is aimed at the Pole Star for a 3-hour exposure. Star A lies very close to the Pole Star in the picture and star B lies far from it. The sky is taken to turn once round the Pole Star in about 24 hours. Which statement about their arcs is correct?
questions.a: Both arcs turn through 45 degrees (3/24 of a full circle), but B's arc is longer because it lies on a bigger circle around the Pole Star.
o: Both arcs turn through 45 degrees, but B's arc is longer because it lies on a bigger circle
A's arc turns through more degrees than B's, because it is near the centre
B's arc turns through more degrees than A's, because it is farther from the Pole Star
Both arcs have the same length, since both stars take 3 hours

questions.q:
Read the statements about the night sky.
1. The Pole Star appears nearly stationary because the Earth's axis of rotation points very close to it.
2. The Moon, like the Sun, appears to rise in the East and set in the West because the Earth rotates from West to East.
3. Over one night the Big Dipper appears to circle the Pole Star because the Earth revolves around the Sun.
questions.a: 1 and 2 only. Statement 3 is false: the circling in one night comes from the Earth's rotation; revolution takes about 365 days and 6 hours.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The stars above Pune appear to move at night because they really travel round the Pole Star.
Reason (R): The Earth's rotation makes the stars appear to move around the nearly stationary Pole Star.
questions.a: A is false but R is true. The stars' circling is apparent, produced by the Earth's rotation.
o: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

questions.q: Taking the sky to turn once round the Pole Star in about 24 hours, a star in a 9-hour exposure sweeps an arc of ___ degrees.
True or False, with a reason or correction: the Pole Star shows up as a dot in a long-exposure photograph because it is very far away, much farther than the other stars.
questions.a: False. All the stars are very far away, yet the others show up as arcs. The Pole Star is a dot because the Earth's axis of rotation points very close to it, so it appears nearly stationary.
s: Verdict: False
Corrects the reason: the axis points close to the Pole Star, distance does not make the difference

questions.q: (a) By how many seconds is Aryabhata's value 23 h 56 min 4.1 s for one rotation shorter than 24 hours? (b) A student counts 30 rotations at 24 hours each. By how much does this total differ from 30 rotations at Aryabhata's value?
s: Part (a): 235.9 seconds
Part (b): 7077 s, which is 1 h 57 min 57 s

questions.q: Cloud hides the Pole Star on the night of Hiba's activity, but she still wants to follow the Big Dipper. (a) What can she use in its place? (b) Why will her sketches still show the Big Dipper moving around a fixed point?
questions.a: (a) A fixed tree or building on the ground in the direction of the Big Dipper, marked with the time on each sketch. (b) The stars appear to move because the Earth rotates, so the movement is there whether or not the Pole Star is visible.
s: Part (a): a fixed tree or building as the reference
Part (b): the movement is due to the Earth's rotation

questions.q: Sunita makes her first sketch on 1 April at 9 pm and her second on 1 May at 9 pm. Tara makes both sketches on the night of 1 April, two hours apart. (a) Whose pair of sketches shows only the effect of the Earth's rotation? (b) Why does the other pair not?
questions.a: (a) Tara's pair. (b) A month later the Earth has moved along its orbit, so the sky at the same clock time is different; Sunita's pair mixes the effect of revolution with rotation.
s: Part (a): Tara's pair
Part (b): a month's revolution changes the sky at a fixed time

questions.q: Differentiate between a star-trail photograph and the sketches of Activity 12.3 as records of the stars' apparent motion: how each is made and what each shows.
questions.a: A star-trail photograph keeps the shutter open for a long time and records each star's path as a continuous arc. In the activity the Big Dipper is drawn at fixed times, two hours apart, so it shows separate positions with times marked, not a continuous path.
s: Photograph: continuous arcs from a long exposure
Sketches: separate positions at marked times, two hours apart

questions.q: Mohan says, 'The Sun and the stars rise and set because of the Earth's rotation, but the Moon rises and sets only because it goes round the Earth.' How much of this is right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The first half is right. The Moon does revolve around the Earth, but its daily rising in the East and setting in the West is also due to the Earth rotating from West to East, as for the Sun and the stars. So the second half is wrong.
s: Verdict: partly right
Accepts the Sun-and-stars part and that the Moon revolves around the Earth
Says the Moon's daily rise and set is also caused by the Earth's rotation

questions.q: A student says the Big Dipper's shift during the ten-hour night activity was caused by the Earth's revolution around the Sun. Taking the revolution as 365.25 days of 24 hours and the rotation as 15 degrees per hour, show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: Revolution in 10 hours covers 10 / (365.25 x 24) of the orbit, which is about 0.41 degrees of the 360. Rotation in 10 hours turns the sky through 10 x 15 = 150 degrees. The shift seen in the sketches is large, so it is the rotation, not the revolution, that explains it.
s: Revolution in 10 hours is about 0.41 degrees of the orbit
Rotation in 10 hours is 150 degrees
Concludes the visible shift comes from rotation

questions.q: Plan a night activity like Activity 12.3 for the Moon. Write what you will record, how often, and what pattern of movement you expect, with its cause.
questions.a: Mark the Moon's position against a fixed tree or building every hour for three hours, writing the time on each sketch. I expect the Moon to appear to move towards the west across the sky, because the Earth rotates from West to East, just as the Sun and the stars appear to.
s: Uses a fixed reference and notes the time on each sketch
Records at regular intervals through the same night
Predicts westward motion and gives the Earth's rotation as the cause

questions.q: Rhea sketches the Big Dipper from 7 pm to 5 am on one night, every two hours. Take the sky to turn once round the Pole Star in about 24 hours. (i) Through how many degrees does it turn in one hour? (ii) Between two successive sketches? (iii) From her first sketch to her last? (iv) Is the Big Dipper then more or less than half way round? (v) Why does the Pole Star stay in nearly the same place on all the sketches?
questions.a: (i) 360 / 24 = 15 degrees per hour. (ii) 15 x 2 = 30 degrees. (iii) 10 hours x 15 = 150 degrees. (iv) 150 is less than 180, so it is less than half way round. (v) The Earth's axis of rotation points very close to the Pole Star, so it appears nearly stationary.
s: 15 degrees per hour
30 degrees between successive sketches
150 degrees from first to last
Less than half way round, since 150 < 180
Pole Star nearly stationary because the axis points close to it

questions.q: A school has a high ceiling but a cloudy sky, and wants to show that the Earth rotates. Compare the Foucault pendulum and a star-trail photograph or the sketches of Activity 12.3 as ways to show this. Say how each is set up, what each shows, and which the school should choose, with a reason.
questions.a: A Foucault pendulum is a long string with a heavy bob hung from a high ceiling; Foucault used it in the middle of the nineteenth century as the first simple demonstration of the Earth's rotation. Star trails need a camera left open for a long time, or sketches every two hours, under a clear sky; they show stars moving round the nearly stationary Pole Star because the Earth rotates. Both are explained by the Earth's rotation. A school with a high ceiling and cloudy nights can choose the pendulum, because it needs no clear sky; a school with a clear dark sky and no tall hall should choose star trails.
s: Pendulum set-up: long string, heavy bob, high ceiling
Pendulum shows the Earth's rotation (Foucault, middle of the nineteenth century)
Star trails or sketches: set-up and what they show around the Pole Star
Both are explained by rotation
Justified choice using the school's ceiling and sky

questions.q:
The astronomy club of a Nashik school plans a poster on the apparent motion of the stars. Taking the sky to turn once round the Pole Star in about 24 hours, the club has two plans for the northern sky. Plan 1: one photograph with the shutter open for 3 hours. Plan 2: six short photographs, each of 30 seconds, taken two hours apart and printed together with their times.
(a) Through how many degrees does a star (other than the Pole Star) sweep in the 3-hour exposure?
(b) What does the tiny dot at the centre of the Plan 1 picture show about the Earth's axis, and what would every star look like if the Earth did not rotate?
(c) By how many degrees do the stars shift between two successive photographs of Plan 2, and how many degrees from the first to the last?
(d) The club has room for only one plan on the poster. Which would you choose to teach Class VII that the motion is only apparent, and what does the other plan show better?
questions.a: (a) 3 x 15 = 45 degrees. (b) The axis points very close to the Pole Star; without rotation every star would be a dot. (c) 2 x 15 = 30 degrees between successive photographs; five gaps of 2 hours = 10 hours = 150 degrees. (d) Either choice with a reason: Plan 1 shows the motion at a glance as continuous arcs; Plan 2 lets viewers read the times and measure how fast the sky turns (30 degrees in 2 hours).
s: Part (a): 45 degrees
Part (b): axis points close to the Pole Star; stars would be dots
Part (c): 30 degrees between photographs, 150 degrees overall
Part (d): a reasoned choice with what the other plan shows better

questions.q:
A ferry crosses a river steadily. Asha, a passenger, sees a lamp-post on the bank slide backwards past her; Ravi, standing on the bank, sees the ferry go forward. A Class VII teacher uses this to explain Verse 9 of the Golapada of the Aryabhatiya, in which a man in a boat sees stationary objects move backwards, so people of Lanka see the stationary stars move towards the west. She also shows the merry-go-round of Activity 12.1 as a second picture.
(a) In the verse, what stands for the boat, for the passenger and for the lamp-post?
(b) In which direction is the Earth turning, according to this explanation, and why does that make the stars appear to go towards the west?
(c) The verse says the stars move towards the west. The Pole Star does not seem to go west. Why not?
(d) The teacher can put only one of the two pictures on the chart: the boat of Aryabhata or the merry-go-round. Which would you choose for the Pole Star and the circling stars, and why?
questions.a: (a) The boat is the Earth, the passenger is the observer on the Earth, the lamp-post is a star. (b) West to East; the observer is carried eastward so the stationary stars appear to go the opposite way, west. (c) The Earth's axis points very close to the Pole Star, so it appears nearly stationary and the others circle it. (d) The merry-go-round: it turns about a centre, so objects appear to go round, with a middle point that hardly moves, matching the circling stars around the Pole Star; the boat gives a straight-line picture and has the historical link to Aryabhata. A reasoned choice earns the mark.
s: Part (a): boat is the Earth, passenger the observer, lamp-post a star
Part (b): West to East, so stars seem to go west
Part (c): axis points close to the Pole Star
Part (d): a reasoned choice using circling around a central point

questions.q: Karan in Ranchi sees a particular group of stars just rising at 10 pm on 5 October. When will he next see that same group just rising at 10 pm?
questions.a: About 5 October next year. The sky seen at a fixed time repeats only when the Earth is back at the same place in its orbit, after about 365 days and 6 hours.
o: About 5 October next year, when the Earth is back at the same place in its orbit
About 5 November, when the Earth has rotated about thirty more times on its own axis
About 5 April, when the Earth is on the opposite side of its orbit from where it was
On the very next night, as soon as the Earth has completed one more rotation

questions.q: Anjali wants to record two evening skies that look as different as possible from each other. She can observe the sky at sunset on 10 June and on one more date. Which second date should she pick?
questions.a: 10 December. Six months later the Earth is on the opposite side of its orbit, so at sunset it looks in the direction farthest from the one in June.
o: 10 December, when the Earth is on the opposite side of its orbit
10 July, when the Earth has moved a month along its orbit
10 September, when the Earth has moved a quarter of the way round
10 June of the next year, when the Earth has completed one revolution

questions.q: A teacher lists four activities. Which one gives evidence of the Earth's revolution rather than its rotation?
questions.a: Noting the pattern of stars at 9 pm on days a month apart. The change over a month comes from the Earth's movement along its orbit; the other three show changes within one night caused by rotation.
o: Noting the pattern of stars at 9 pm on days a month apart
Sketching the Big Dipper every two hours through one night
Leaving a camera shutter open for three hours aimed at the Pole Star
Watching the Moon climb from the eastern horizon during one evening

questions.q: Mina's Class VI textbook drew the Earth's orbit as a long flat oval. She argues, 'So the Earth must be much nearer the Sun in some months than in others, and this explains why the sky changes.' Which reply fits this chapter?
questions.a: Seen from the top the orbit is nearly circular; the oval look comes from a side view, and the sky changes because the Earth's place on its orbit changes the direction we look at night.
o: Seen from the top the orbit is nearly circular; the oval was a side view, and the sky changes because we look in different directions

Part (b): -6, +8 and -10 days
Part (c): the pattern is more regular, spread 1 day against 17
Part (d): a reasoned decision weighing the regular marker against the varying rains

questions.q:
Match each event for Delhi or the North Pole in Column A with its date and name in Column B.
Column A:
1. Delhi's longest daytime of the year
2. Delhi has 12 hours of daytime in the month of September
3. Delhi's shortest daytime of the year
4. The Sun first rises at the North Pole after months of darkness
Column B:
a. Around 23 September, the autumn equinox
b. Around 21 June, the summer solstice
c. Around 22 December, the winter solstice
d. Around 21 March, the equinox day
questions.a: 1-b, 2-a, 3-c, 4-d. The longest day is the summer solstice, 12 hours in September is the autumn equinox, the shortest day is the winter solstice and the polar Sun first rises on 21 March.

questions.q: On 21 June, when the North Pole has 24 hours of sunlight, a station at the South Pole has ___ hours of sunlight.
True or False, with a reason or correction: on 21 June, the longest day in Delhi, a town on the equator has 12 hours of daytime, the same as on 22 December.
questions.a: True. On the equator there are always 12 hours of sunlight and 12 hours of darkness, so 21 June is not a longest day there; its day length stays the same all through the year.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the equator always has 12 hours of daytime

questions.q: (a) How many days are there from the summer solstice (21 June) to the autumn equinox (23 September) in a year of 365 days? (b) During these days, how does Delhi's daytime change, and at what value does it end?
questions.a: (a) 9 + 31 + 31 + 23 = 94 days. (b) Daytime keeps getting shorter and ends at 12 hours on the autumn equinox.
s: Part (a): 94 days
Part (b): shortens and ends at 12 hours

questions.q: At a North Pole station the Sun sets on 22 September. (a) What does a South Pole station see around that date? (b) How many hours of daytime does a station on the equator have that day?
questions.a: (a) The South Pole has the opposite behaviour, so its Sun begins to rise and stay in the sky. (b) 12 hours; the equator always has 12 hours of sunlight and 12 hours of darkness.
s: Part (a): opposite behaviour, sunshine begins at the South Pole
Part (b): 12 hours at the equator

questions.q: Differentiate between a solstice and an equinox by giving, for the Northern Hemisphere, an approximate date and the length of daytime for each kind.
questions.a: Solstice: around 21 June (summer solstice, the longest day) and around 22 December (winter solstice, the shortest day). Equinox: around 21 March and 23 September, when daytime lasts 12 hours.
s: Solstice: around 21 June longest day and around 22 December shortest day
Equinox: around 21 March and 23 September, daytime 12 hours

questions.q: Dev says, 'Chennai and Srinagar are both in the Northern Hemisphere, so they must feel the same seasons.' (a) What does the chapter say about the effect of seasons in the southern states of India? (b) Name one other influence it gives that can change the pattern.
questions.a: (a) The effect of seasons is not very prominent there, because they lie close to the equator, where daytime is about 12 hours and sunray intensity changes little. (b) Local geographical features, or nearness to oceans or seas.
s: Part (a): seasons not prominent near the equator, with the reason
Part (b): local geography or nearness to a sea

questions.q: Zoya says, 'At the North Pole the Sun rises on 21 March and sets on 22 September, so counting the days gives a stretch of nearly six months of continuous sunshine.' Is she right? Count the days for a year of 365 days.
questions.a: Yes. From 21 March to 22 September is 10 + 30 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 31 + 22 = 185 days, about 6.2 months of 30 days, so 'nearly six months' is right. The polar regions have continuous sunshine for six months followed by six months of darkness.
s: Verdict: right
Counts 185 days
Links 185 days to about six months of sunshine, then darkness

questions.q: A camp report says the Sun was in the sky for all 24 hours at the North Pole on 10 December. Show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The Sun sets at the North Pole around 22 September and stays down for the next six months. In December the Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun and the North Pole is in darkness for all 24 hours. So the report for 10 December must be wrong.
s: Sun sets around 22 September and is down for six months
In December the North Pole is in darkness for 24 hours
Concludes the report is wrong

questions.q: Write four diary entries of Delhi's daytime, for 21 March, 21 June, 23 September and 22 December, that are consistent with the chapter. Give the length of daytime in each entry and the name of the day.
questions.a: For example: 21 March, 12 h, spring equinox. 21 June, 13 h 45 min, summer solstice, the longest day. 23 September, 12 h, autumn equinox. 22 December, 10 h 15 min, winter solstice, the shortest day. Any figures with 21 June the longest, 22 December the shortest and the equinoxes 12 h are acceptable.
s: The two equinox entries are 12 hours
21 June is the longest day, named summer solstice
22 December is the shortest day, named winter solstice

questions.q: A student records Delhi's daytime (invented data): 21 March, 12 h 00 min; 21 June, 13 h 45 min; 23 September, 12 h 00 min; 22 December, 10 h 15 min. (i) Which are the solstice dates? (ii) By how much do the longest and shortest days differ? (iii) How long is the longest night of the year? (iv) What would the equator's table look like? (v) On 21 June, is Hobart's daytime longer or shorter than 12 hours, and why?
questions.a: (i) 21 June, the summer solstice, and 22 December, the winter solstice. (ii) 13 h 45 min - 10 h 15 min = 3 h 30 min. (iii) 24 h - 10 h 15 min = 13 h 45 min, on 22 December. (iv) The equator would show 12 h 00 min on all four dates, a difference of zero. (v) Shorter than 12 hours: day length is reversed in the Southern Hemisphere, which is tilted away from the Sun in June.
s: Solstice dates 21 June and 22 December
Difference of 3 h 30 min
Longest night 13 h 45 min
Equator: 12 h on all four dates
Hobart in June: shorter than 12 hours, reversed in the south

questions.q: At the North Pole the Sun rises on 21 March and sets on 22 September. For a year of 365 days find (i) the days of sunshine, (ii) the days of darkness, (iii) how many more days of sunshine than darkness the North Pole has, and (iv) the days of sunshine at the South Pole. (v) What do your answers show about the 'six months of sunshine and six months of darkness' at the poles?
questions.a: (i) 185 days. (ii) 365 - 185 = 180 days. (iii) 185 - 180 = 5 days more. (iv) The South Pole has the opposite behaviour, so its sunshine is the North Pole's darkness: 180 days. (v) Each pole has about six months of each, though not exactly equal, and the two poles are opposite: when one has sunshine the other has darkness.
s: 185 days of sunshine
180 days of darkness
5 more days of sunshine than darkness
South Pole sunshine is 180 days, the opposite of the North
Roughly six months each, opposite at the two poles

questions.q:
A polar research programme has two teams. Team N works at the North Pole and Team S at the South Pole. Each experiment needs the Sun to be in the sky continuously for at least 150 days from the day it starts. The North Pole has sunshine from 21 March to 22 September, and the South Pole has the opposite behaviour. Use a year of 365 days, with the South Pole season running to 21 March of the next year.
(a) How many days of sunshine remain at the North Pole if Team N starts on 1 April?
(b) How many days of sunshine remain at the South Pole if Team S starts on 1 October?
(c) What would Team S find if it started on 1 April?
(d) Find the latest start date for each team that still gives 150 days, and say which of 1 April and 1 October each team should choose if only these two dates can be used.
questions.a: (a) 1 April to 22 September is 174 days. (b) 1 October to 21 March is 171 days. (c) Darkness: the South Pole is in its six months of darkness then. (d) Team N: latest start 150 days before 22 September, which is 25 April; Team S: 150 days before 21 March, which is 22 October. With only the two dates, Team N should choose 1 April and Team S 1 October; both give more than 150 days.
s: Part (a): 174 days
Part (b): 171 days
Part (c): darkness at the South Pole in April
Part (d): latest starts 25 April and 22 October; choose 1 April for N and 1 October for S

questions.q:
A Delhi school plans a 5-hour outdoor festival that needs sunset to come at least 30 minutes after the festival ends. It can be held on one of four dates. The table gives sunrise and sunset in Delhi (rounded, invented for the exercise). 21 March: 6:30 am, 6:30 pm. 21 June: 5:25 am, 7:20 pm. 23 September: 6:20 am, 6:20 pm. 22 December: 7:10 am, 5:30 pm.
(a) Find the daytime on each date and name each date as a solstice or an equinox.
(b) If the festival must start at 1:45 pm, which dates leave the 30-minute margin?
(c) If the festival can instead start at 12:30 pm, which dates leave the margin?
(d) For the 12:30 pm start the school must pick one date. Compare the best two options using the chapter and recommend one.
questions.a: (a) 21 March 12 h (equinox); 21 June 13 h 55 min (summer solstice); 23 September 12 h (equinox); 22 December 10 h 20 min (winter solstice). (b) The festival ends at 6:45 pm, so sunset must be at 7:15 pm or later: only 21 June (7:20 pm). (c) It ends at 5:30 pm, so sunset must be at 6:00 pm or later: 21 March, 21 June and 23 September; not 22 December (sunset 5:30 pm). (d) Either 21 June or an equinox date with a reason: 21 June gives the longest daylight and the biggest margin (1 h 50 min), but in June the Northern Hemisphere gets its most intense sunlight; an equinox date leaves a margin of 50 minutes to 1 hour, with less intense sunlight. Any recommendation backed by these two facts earns the mark.
s: Part (a): 12 h, 13 h 55 min, 12 h, 10 h 20 min with solstice or equinox names
Part (b): only 21 June
Part (c): 21 March, 21 June and 23 September
Part (d): a recommendation weighing margin against sunlight intensity

questions.q: Suppose the Moon were moved much farther from the Earth while its physical size stayed the same. What would change about solar eclipses?
o: Its apparent size would shrink, so it could no longer hide the whole Sun
Its apparent size would grow, so it would hide the Sun for longer
Its apparent size would stay the same because its physical size is unchanged
It would hide the Sun more completely because farther objects look larger
questions.a: Its apparent size would shrink, so it could no longer hide the whole Sun -- apparent size depends on both physical size and distance.

questions.q: In a dark hall a lamp 30 cm across stands 15 m from Rohan. A ball 6 cm across, held 3 m from his eye, just hides the lamp. Take apparent size to be proportional to actual size divided by distance. He now moves the same ball to 4.5 m from his eye, in line with the lamp. What does he see?
questions.a: The ball no longer hides the whole lamp. Its ratio is 0.06/4.5, about 0.013, which is less than the lamp's 0.30/15 = 0.02, so a rim of the lamp shows around it.
o: The ball no longer hides the whole lamp; a rim of the lamp shows around it
The ball still just hides the lamp, since its size has not changed at all
The ball hides the lamp even more completely, since it is now farther from his eye
The ball and the lamp both look larger than before, as he has moved the ball

questions.q: A school on a hill has 12 pairs of eclipse goggles for 60 students and one teacher-run mirror projection set. Which plan for the solar eclipse is safe for all 60?
questions.a: Students take turns with the goggles, and the rest watch the projected image on a screen. The chapter warns against viewing through sunglasses, binoculars or telescopes and against direct viewing.
o: Students take turns with the goggles, and the rest watch the projected image on a screen
Everyone wears dark sunglasses, since the eclipse has made the Sun dimmer
Students take turns using binoculars, which the teacher has brought along
Students look straight at the Sun only during the dark minutes of totality

questions.q: Take apparent size as proportional to actual size divided by distance, with these rounded figures. Moon: 3,500 km across at 3,84,000 km. Sun: 14,00,000 km across at 15,00,00,000 km. Venus: 12,000 km across at 4,00,00,000 km at a transit. Which conclusion matches the chapter?
questions.a: The Moon's ratio is about 0.0091 and the Sun's 0.0093, nearly equal, while Venus's is 0.0003, about one-thirtieth of the Sun's. So the Moon can cover the Sun, and Venus appears only as a tiny dot.
o: The Moon looks about as big as the Sun, but Venus looks only about one-thirtieth of the Sun's size
The Moon looks about one-thirtieth of the Sun's size, but Venus looks as big as the Sun
Venus looks bigger than the Moon, since it is physically larger than the Moon
All three look about equally large, since the three ratios are nearly equal

questions.q: Arman watches a total solar eclipse with his class and says, 'This darkness at midday is the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon.' Which reply is correct?
questions.a: No; the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth and its shadow falls on a small area of the Earth. The Earth's shadow on the Moon is a lunar eclipse.
o: No; the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth, and its shadow falls on a small area
No; the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, and its shadow falls on the whole Earth
Yes; at midday the Earth is always between the Sun and the Moon
Yes; the Earth's shadow reaches only a small area, which is why it is brief

questions.q:
Read the statements about eclipses.
1. Venus is larger than the Moon, so a Transit of Venus hides more of the Sun than a solar eclipse does.
2. Dark sunglasses make it safe to look at the Sun during an eclipse, because the Moon cuts down the Sun's light.
3. The Moon is much smaller than the Sun but looks about as large from the Earth because it is much closer.
questions.a: 3 only. In statement 1 Venus is far away and shows only as a tiny black dot; in statement 2 the Sun is intense enough to damage the eyes even during an eclipse.
o: 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Dark sunglasses are not a safe way to watch a solar eclipse.
Reason (R): Even during an eclipse the Sun is intense enough to damage the eyes.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. The Sun remains intense, so sunglasses do not make direct viewing safe.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A

A is false but R is true

questions.q: A ball 12 cm across just hides the same 30 cm lamp that stands 15 m from the eye, taking apparent size as actual size divided by distance. The ball must be held ___ m from the eye.
True or False, with a reason or correction: because the Moon is much smaller than the Sun in physical size, it must also look much smaller than the Sun in the sky.
questions.a: False. Apparent size depends on both physical size and distance. The Moon is much closer to us, so its apparent size is similar to that of the Sun, which is why it can cover the Sun in a total solar eclipse.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: apparent size depends on distance as well, and the Moon is much closer

questions.q: A thumb 2 cm wide held 50 cm from the eye just covers a friend's head 20 cm wide. Take apparent size as proportional to actual size divided by distance. (a) How far away is the friend? (b) If the friend steps back to twice that distance, will the thumb still cover the head? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Thumb ratio 2/50 = 0.04, so the head 20 cm needs 20/0.04 = 500 cm = 5 m. (b) Yes. At 10 m the head's ratio falls to 20/1000 = 0.02, so it looks smaller than the thumb and is still covered.
s: Part (a): 5 m
Part (b): yes, the head looks smaller than the thumb

questions.q: Differentiate between a total solar eclipse and a Transit of Venus: what comes between the Sun and the Earth, what is seen of the Sun, and why.
questions.a: In a total solar eclipse the Moon comes between and no part of the Sun is seen from the area of its shadow, because the Moon's apparent size is similar to the Sun's. In a Transit of Venus, Venus appears as a tiny black dot on the bright Sun, because Venus is much farther and its apparent size is very small.
s: Total solar eclipse: Moon hides the Sun, apparent sizes similar
Transit: Venus only a tiny black dot, because it is much farther

questions.q: Meera plans to project the eclipse onto the wall of the school corridor with her mother's make-up mirror, aimed down a staircase where friends are standing. Name two changes the chapter calls for.
questions.a: She should do it only under the strict supervision of a teacher, and take care that the reflected beam is not directed into anyone's eyes.
s: Under the supervision of a teacher
Do not direct the reflected light beam into anyone's eyes

questions.q: During one eclipse Asha, standing in the Moon's shadow, sees the day turn dark, while Bharat, standing where the Moon blocks only some regions of the Sun, does not. (a) Why does Bharat not see the day turn dark? (b) Why does Asha's darkness last only a few minutes?
questions.a: (a) Part of the Sun is still visible to him, so sunlight still reaches his place. (b) The Moon's shadow moves across the Earth's surface because of the Earth's rotation and the Moon's motion in its orbit, so it soon passes Asha's place.
s: Part (a): part of the Sun still visible, sunlight still reaches him
Part (b): the shadow moves because of rotation and the Moon's motion

questions.q: Sana says, 'A total solar eclipse is seen only from a small area of the Earth, and nobody outside that small area sees any part of the Sun hidden.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: No. The first half is right: the Moon's shadow falls on a small area, and only there is the eclipse total. The second half is wrong: observers where the Moon blocks only some regions of the Sun see a partial solar eclipse, so some of the Sun is hidden for them too.
s: Verdict: disagrees with the claim as a whole
Accepts that totality is seen only in the small shadow area
Corrects: where the Moon blocks only some regions, a partial eclipse is seen

questions.q: Show that a total solar eclipse cannot be seen at the same moment from every place on the daylit side of the Earth.
questions.a: The Moon's shadow falls on only a small area of the Earth's surface, and only observers in that area see no part of the Sun. Observers where the Moon blocks only some regions of the Sun see a partial eclipse. So at any moment most daylit places cannot see the Sun totally hidden.
s: The Moon's shadow falls on only a small area
Only observers in that area see a total eclipse
Others see a partial eclipse, so not every place sees totality

questions.q: Write two short situations: one in which an observer sees a total solar eclipse and one in which a different observer sees a partial solar eclipse at the same time. Say where each stands.
questions.a: Total: Asha stands in the small area on the Earth where the Moon's shadow falls and sees no part of the Sun. Partial: Bharat stands in a region where the Moon blocks only some regions of the Sun and sees part of the Sun still shining. Neither looks at the Sun directly.
s: Total: observer inside the Moon's shadow area, no part of the Sun seen
Partial: observer where the Moon blocks only some regions of the Sun
Places the two observers in different regions at the same time

questions.q: A lamp 30 cm across stands 15 m from Rohan, who holds balls in line with it. Take apparent size as proportional to actual size divided by distance. (i) A ball 6 cm across: at what distance does it just hide the lamp? (ii) A ball 18 cm across: at what distance does it just hide the lamp? (iii) The 18 cm ball is placed 30 m from Rohan. Does it hide the lamp? (iv) Which of the balls stands for the Moon and which for Venus? Give the reason.
questions.a: (i) The lamp's ratio is 0.30/15 = 0.02; 6 cm ball: 0.06/0.02 = 3 m. (ii) 0.18/0.02 = 9 m. (iii) Its ratio is 0.18/30 = 0.006, less than 0.02, so it does not hide the lamp. (iv) The small ball held close stands for the Moon, much smaller than the Sun but much closer; the big ball far away stands for Venus, larger than the Moon but much farther, so it looks small and does not hide the Sun.
s: 3 m for the small ball
9 m for the big ball
0.006 is less than 0.02, so the far ball does not hide the lamp
Small close ball stands for the Moon
Large far ball stands for Venus, because of distance

questions.q: A school of 600 students gets 40 pairs of eclipse goggles for a 90-minute viewing slot. (i) How many goggle-minutes are available? (ii) What is the average goggle time per student? (iii) The principal wants every student to get 10 minutes with goggles. Is that possible? (iv) Name the other safe method the chapter gives to include everyone. (v) Name three ways of viewing the school must ban, with one reason.
questions.a: (i) 40 x 90 = 3600 goggle-minutes. (ii) 3600 / 600 = 6 minutes per student. (iii) No: 600 x 10 = 6000 goggle-minutes are needed, more than 3600. (iv) Mirror projection of the Sun's image onto a wall or screen, set up under a teacher's supervision. (v) Direct viewing, sunglasses, binoculars or telescopes; even during the eclipse the Sun is intense enough to damage the eyes.
s: 3600 goggle-minutes
6 minutes per student
10 minutes each is impossible: 6000 needed
Mirror projection under supervision includes everyone
Bans direct viewing, sunglasses, binoculars or telescopes, with the reason

questions.q:
Class VII has 30 students at a 45-minute eclipse viewing. The planetarium organisers lent 10 pairs of eclipse goggles, but 2 are found damaged and cannot be used. The teacher also has one mirror-projection set up on a screen that the whole class can watch together. The rule is that every student gets at least 10 minutes of viewing with goggles or the projection.
(a) How many usable pairs are there, and how many goggle-minutes are available in 45 minutes?
(b) If each turn lasts 10 minutes, how many turns are needed for all 30 students on the goggles alone, and does it fit in 45 minutes?
(c) How many viewing minutes would each student get from the projection if everyone watched it for the whole 45 minutes?
(d) The teacher can run either the goggle rota alone or the projection alone. Weigh the two and recommend one.
questions.a: (a) 8 pairs; 8 x 45 = 360 goggle-minutes. (b) 30/8 = 3.75, so 4 turns, taking 40 minutes, which fits. (c) 45 minutes. (d) Either, with a reason: the rota gives each student 10 minutes of a direct view, but only 8 watch at once and the rest wait; the projection lets all 30 watch together for the whole time but only as an indirect image and it must be run under the teacher's strict supervision. A recommendation backed by these points earns the mark.
s: Part (a): 8 pairs and 360 goggle-minutes
Part (b): 4 turns, 40 minutes
Part (c): 45 minutes each
Part (d): a reasoned recommendation weighing the two methods

questions.q:
In a village near Madurai, Naani says nobody should eat, cook or step out of the house during a solar eclipse. The next eclipse is at lunchtime. Her grandson Pranav's class has studied eclipses. A planetarium holds a public viewing event 20 km away, with eye protection and a talk. Pranav's family can either go to the event or stay at home and have lunch as usual, without looking at the Sun.
(a) What causes a solar eclipse?
(b) Why were such restrictions placed in the past, and what does the chapter say we need not fear?
(c) Which one precaution still applies in both plans?
(d) Compare the two plans and advise the family.
questions.a: (a) The Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth and blocks the sunlight from reaching us. (b) People did not know the reason and feared something blocking the Sun, the main source of heat and light; now that we know why it happens, we need not fear it as long as we do not look at the Sun directly. (c) Never look directly at the Sun, nor through sunglasses, binoculars or telescopes. (d) Either, with reasons: the event is the best way to observe because organisers give eye protection and scientific explanations, but means a 20 km trip at lunchtime; staying home is safe if no one looks at the Sun, but misses the explanation.
s: Part (a): the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth
Part (b): fear from not knowing the cause; no fear if the Sun is not viewed directly
Part (c): no direct viewing, nor through sunglasses, binoculars or telescopes
Part (d): a reasoned comparison and advice

questions.q: Three bodies lie in one line, with the Sun at one end. Observers on the body C at the other end see the Sun completely hidden by the middle body B for a few minutes, and only within a small area of C. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: B is the Moon and C is the Earth. The Sun is hidden only within the small area where the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth, which is a total solar eclipse.
o: B is the Moon and C is the Earth, and the observers are in the Moon's shadow
B is the Earth and C is the Moon, and the observers are in the Earth's shadow
B is Venus and C is the Earth, and the observers are in Venus's shadow
B is the Moon and C is the Earth, and the observers are in the Earth's shadow

questions.q: Why can people over a large part of the night side of the Earth watch the same lunar eclipse, while a total solar eclipse is seen from only a small area?
questions.a: The Earth's shadow falls on the whole disc of the Moon, but the Moon's shadow falls on only a small area of the Earth. This is why a lunar eclipse is seen from a large part of the Earth.
o: The Earth's shadow covers the whole Moon, but the Moon's shadow falls on a small area of the Earth
The Moon is bigger than the Earth, so its shadow is larger than the Earth's shadow and covers more
A lunar eclipse lasts only a few minutes, while a total solar eclipse goes on for several hours
The Sun is nearer to the Moon than to the Earth, so its light bends round the Earth and spreads

questions.q: Ritu wants real records of how the Sun has looked over more than a hundred years for a school project. Which source fits what the chapter says?
questions.a: The Kodaikanal Solar Observatory. It was established in 1899, has given data about the Sun for over 100 years and is operated by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics, Bengaluru.
o: The Kodaikanal Solar Observatory, set up in 1899 and run by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics
The Kavalur observatory, named after a scientist who mainly studied stars
A Foucault pendulum, whose swing records the Sun's changes
The Stellarium app, which only lists the dates of coming eclipses

questions.q: Over one night the Moon passes through the Earth's shadow and a total lunar eclipse happens. In which order do the stages appear?

The whole Moon looks dark red at once, then the shadow disappears from all of it at the same instant
The whole Moon is in the shadow and dark red, then part of the Moon is in the shadow, then it is dark red again
Part of the Moon is in the shadow, then the Moon looks bright, then it looks dark red as it leaves

questions.q:
Read the statements about eclipses of the Moon.

2. In a lunar eclipse the Earth's shadow falls on only a small area, so very few people can see it.

1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A lunar eclipse occurs when the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth.
Reason (R): In a lunar eclipse the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
questions.a: A is false but R is true. In a lunar eclipse the Earth lies between the Sun and the Moon; the Moon in the middle gives a solar eclipse.

Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

A is true but R is false

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column A with the event it shows in Column B.

1. The whole Moon lies in the Earth's shadow and looks dark red

questions.q: Standing on the Moon during a total lunar eclipse, an astronaut who looks towards the Sun would see it hidden by the ___.
questions.a: Earth

questions.q: True or False, with a reason or correction: in a lunar eclipse and in a solar eclipse the Sun, the Earth and the Moon lie roughly along one line, but the body in the middle is different.
questions.a: True. In a lunar eclipse the Earth is in the middle (Sun, Earth, Moon), blocking sunlight from the Moon. In a solar eclipse the Moon is in the middle (Sun, Moon, Earth), blocking sunlight from the Earth.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the Earth is in the middle for a lunar eclipse and the Moon for a solar eclipse

questions.q: M.K. Vainu Bappu travelled to different parts of the world to study solar eclipses. (a) Why must an astronomer travel to see a total solar eclipse? (b) Would the same travel be needed to see a total lunar eclipse? Explain.
questions.a: (a) The Moon's shadow falls on only a small area of the Earth, so totality is seen only from there. (b) No; the Earth's shadow falls on the full disc of the Moon, so a lunar eclipse can be seen from a large part of the Earth.
s: Part (a): totality is seen only in a small area
Part (b): not needed, a lunar eclipse is seen from a large part of the Earth

questions.q: Differentiate between a total and a partial lunar eclipse in terms of where the Moon is relative to the Earth's shadow and what is seen.
questions.a: Total: the Moon is completely in the Earth's shadow and its bright disc appears dark red until it moves out of the shadow. Partial: only part of the Moon is in the Earth's shadow and the rest of the Moon remains visible.
s: Total: completely in the shadow, dark red
Partial: part in the shadow, the rest visible

questions.q: The Kodaikanal Solar Observatory was established in 1899 and has provided data about the Sun for over 100 years. (a) For how many years had it been operating by 2025? (b) If it had made one record every day for these years (assume 365 days a year), about how many records would it hold?
s: Part (a): 126 years
Part (b): 45,990, about 46,000 records

questions.q: Priya's cousin says, 'Last night's total lunar eclipse happened because the Moon came between the Sun and the Earth, and the Moon looked completely black.' Correct the two mistakes.
questions.a: In a lunar eclipse the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon and its shadow falls on the Moon; it is in a solar eclipse that the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth. In a total lunar eclipse the bright disc of the Moon appears dark red, not black.
s: Corrects the line-up: the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon
Corrects the colour: dark red

questions.q: Hari says, 'During a total lunar eclipse the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon and people over a large part of the Earth see it at the same time, and the Moon looks completely black.' How much of this is right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. The first part is right: the Earth's shadow falls on the full disc of the Moon and, because the Earth's shadow is large, the eclipse is seen from a large part of the Earth. The last part is wrong: in a total lunar eclipse the bright disc of the Moon appears dark red, not black, until it moves out of the shadow.
s: Verdict: partly right
Accepts the Earth's shadow on the Moon and the large area of visibility
Corrects the colour to dark red

questions.q: Show that a total solar eclipse and a total lunar eclipse cannot be happening at the same moment.
questions.a: In a total solar eclipse the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth. In a total lunar eclipse the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. The Moon is at one place in its orbit at any moment, so it cannot be between the Sun and the Earth and also behind the Earth at the same time.
s: Solar eclipse needs the Moon between the Sun and the Earth
Lunar eclipse needs the Earth between the Sun and the Moon
The Moon cannot be in both positions at once

questions.q: Write two questions from this chapter, with answers, one whose answer is 'the Earth's shadow' and one whose answer is 'the Moon's shadow'. Say what an observer sees in each case.
questions.a: Q1: What falls on the Moon during a lunar eclipse? The Earth's shadow; the Moon appears dark red when it is completely inside it. Q2: What falls on a small area of the Earth during a total solar eclipse? The Moon's shadow; observers there see the Sun completely hidden for a few minutes.
s: A correct question whose answer is the Earth's shadow, with what is seen
A correct question whose answer is the Moon's shadow, with what is seen
Keeps the two events distinct (which body is in the middle)

questions.q: Three students report what they saw. Asha: 'On Tuesday night the full Moon turned dark red for a long time, and we watched from the terrace with no protection.' Bimal: 'On Friday noon the day turned dark for two minutes, and I watched through dark sunglasses.' Chandu: 'At the same noon, in a village 30 km away, I saw part of the Sun covered, but the day did not turn dark.' (i) Name each event. (ii) Judge the safety of each student's method. (iii) Explain why Bimal and Chandu saw different things.
questions.a: (i) Asha saw a total lunar eclipse; Bimal a total solar eclipse; Chandu a partial solar eclipse. (ii) Asha's method is safe, since the eclipsed full Moon can be watched with the naked eye. Bimal's is unsafe, since the Sun is intense enough to damage the eyes and sunglasses do not protect; he should use goggles or mirror projection. Chandu, if he looked directly, was also unsafe. (iii) Bimal was inside the small area covered by the Moon's shadow, where no part of the Sun can be seen; Chandu was where the Moon blocked only some regions of the Sun, so part of the Sun still shone.
s: Names the three events correctly
Asha's method judged safe, with the reason
Bimal's method judged unsafe, with a safe alternative
Chandu's direct viewing, if any, also unsafe
Explains total against partial by the Moon's shadow area

questions.q: You have a torch, a globe and a small ball for a model of eclipses. Describe how you would arrange them to show (i) a solar eclipse and (ii) a lunar eclipse. Say what each object stands for, where the shadow falls in each case, and why the shadow covers only a small area of the globe in one model but the whole ball in the other.
questions.a: The torch is the Sun, the globe the Earth and the ball the Moon. (i) Put the ball between the torch and the globe: the ball's shadow falls on a small area of the globe; observers there see a total solar eclipse. (ii) Put the globe between the torch and the ball: the globe's shadow falls on the whole ball, a lunar eclipse. The Moon's shadow reaches the Earth as a small area because the Moon is much smaller than the Earth; the Earth's shadow is large enough to cover the whole Moon. For the real events, only the solar eclipse needs eye protection; the lunar eclipse can be watched with the naked eye.
s: Torch, globe and ball identified as Sun, Earth and Moon
Solar eclipse: ball between torch and globe, a small area in shadow
Lunar eclipse: globe between torch and ball, whole ball in shadow
Explains small area against whole ball by the sizes of the shadows
Notes the real solar eclipse needs protection, the lunar does not

questions.q:
A Hyderabad housing society of 200 residents has Rs 6,000 for eclipse viewing. A total lunar eclipse is due in March and a total solar eclipse in September, both visible from the town. Eclipse goggles cost Rs 150 a pair. A planetarium offers a supervised mirror-projection screen for Rs 5,500. The partial phases of the solar eclipse last 90 minutes in all.
(a) In which order are the Sun, Earth and Moon in line for each eclipse?
(b) How many pairs of goggles can the society buy, and how many turns are needed for 200 residents if each pair is worn by one person at a time?
(c) Which of the two eclipses needs protective equipment, and why not the other?
(d) The society can choose either the goggles or the projection screen for the September eclipse. Weigh the two and recommend one.
questions.a: (a) Lunar: Sun, Earth, Moon. Solar: Sun, Moon, Earth. (b) 6000/150 = 40 pairs; 200/40 = 5 turns. (c) The solar eclipse; the eclipsed full Moon can be watched with the naked eye. (d) Either with reasons: goggles give each resident a direct view in 5 turns (for 10 minutes each that is 50 minutes, within the 90), but 160 people wait each turn; the screen lets everyone watch at once but is an indirect image, costs nearly the whole budget and must be supervised. A reasoned recommendation earns the mark.
s: Part (a): Sun, Earth, Moon and Sun, Moon, Earth
Part (b): 40 pairs and 5 turns
Part (c): only the solar eclipse needs protection
Part (d): a reasoned recommendation weighing the two options

questions.q:
On the night of a total lunar eclipse, friends Ashok in Pune and Bela in Jaipur, 1,200 km apart and both under clear night sky, each watch the dark red Moon. A month earlier, the Moon's shadow had passed over Jaipur during a total solar eclipse, while Ashok in Pune saw only a part of the Sun covered. Next year a total solar eclipse is expected only along a narrow path through a city 900 km from Pune, while a lunar eclipse will be visible from Pune itself. They have money for one trip.
(a) Which body's shadow falls on which body in each of the two eclipses?
(b) Why could both friends watch the lunar eclipse but only Bela see the total solar eclipse?
(c) What did Ashok see in the solar eclipse, and what protection did he need?
(d) Advise the friends: take the 900 km trip for the solar eclipse or stay in Pune for the lunar eclipse?
questions.a: (a) Lunar: the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. Solar: the Moon's shadow falls on a small area of the Earth. (b) The Earth's shadow covers the whole Moon, so everyone on the night side with the Moon in view sees the lunar eclipse; the Moon's shadow covers only a small area, which was over Jaipur. (c) A partial solar eclipse; goggles or a supervised mirror projection, never direct viewing. (d) Either with reasons: the trip is needed because totality is seen only in the narrow path, and with protection it can be seen for a few minutes; staying home costs nothing and the lunar eclipse needs no protection, but it is a different event. A reasoned recommendation earns the mark.
s: Part (a): Earth's shadow on the Moon; Moon's shadow on a small area of the Earth
Part (b): size of the shadow areas explains who sees what
Part (c): a partial eclipse, with safe viewing methods
Part (d): a reasoned recommendation using the chapter
